transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today?

Yeah, hey doc. Um... well, I guess I'm here because what started as just me trying to eat cleaner for the lieutenant track has sort of... escalated, I guess. The lieutenant track is super competitive right now, by the way. We've got like three guys going for one spot at my station, and this one guy on C shift has been kissing up to the chief like you wouldn't believe. It's honestly kind of embarrassing to watch. 

But anyway, you gotta be in top physical shape to lead, right? So I started watching my food. But now it's turned into me cutting my meals way down to just... I don't know, things like black coffee. Which, to be fair, the coffee at the firehouse is basically motor oil, but you drink it anyway because you're up at 3 AM for false alarms half the time. So just black coffee, maybe a protein shake, and a really small dinner. And I'm doing that even on shift days. I mean, we had a huge structure fire last Tuesday, hauling like fifty pounds of turnout gear around, so I know I burned way more than what I ate that day. But I just kept it to the shake and the small dinner. So, yeah... I guess my captain noticed and suggested I come talk to someone.
Have you been avoiding eating certain foods or cutting back on calories because you're worried about gaining weight, even if others might tell you that you're not overweight?

Yeah, I mean... absolutely. It's like, if I step on the scale and it's up even a single pound—maybe after one of those huge station dinners, or even if I just drank a bunch of water—I get this tight, awful panic in my chest. Like I've completely blown it, you know? And then I start thinking everyone's gonna look at me and think I'm getting soft, or that I've lost control. Which is crazy because at the station, they cook these massive meals. Like, last shift, Miller made his famous baked ziti. The guy uses like three pounds of cheese in one pan. And he's always trying to push seconds on everyone. He's a good guy, Miller, but man, he never shuts up about his fantasy football team. I mean, we get it, you drafted Patrick Mahomes, but you don't have to bring it up every time we sit down to eat. And then there's the rookie, always trying to eat more than everyone else to prove something... but yeah, I just get so freaked out about gaining any weight at all, no matter what anyone else says.
After eating, do you ever make yourself exercise a lot, make yourself vomit, take laxatives, or try to 'undo' what you ate in any way?

No, I don't do any of that stuff. I mean, I don't throw up or take pills or whatever. I definitely work out a lot, but that's just part of the job, you know? Like, we have this gym set up in the back of the apparatus bay. It's actually pretty decent now because we finally got the city to approve the budget for a new squat rack. The old one was literally rusting away, and the safety pins were totally bent from when one of the guys from B shift dropped like four hundred pounds on it. That guy, man... he thinks he's a powerlifter but his form is absolute garbage. He's going to blow out a disc one of these days, I swear. Anyway, yeah, I work out to stay fit for the job, but I don't do it to, like, undo what I ate or anything. I just try to not eat much in the first place.
When you're concerned about eating and gaining weight, is it mainly about keeping your performance up for the job, or is it also about how you see your body or how you think others see it?

Um, I mean, the job is definitely part of it, but... honestly, it's a lot about how I see myself, too. Like, when I look in the mirror before work, I'm constantly checking to see if my waist and face look sharp enough. And if they don't, if I look even a little bit soft, it totally messes with my head. I just don't feel confident or command-ready for the day. Which is huge when you're trying to step up for lieutenant. 

Speaking of the lieutenant exam, the study materials they gave us this year are a total joke. They changed the whole curriculum on building construction, and now half the manual is just these weird, outdated case studies from the 80s. Like, who even uses that specific type of truss roof anymore? I was talking to Captain Harris about it, and he said back when he took the test, they actually had to draw the load-bearing walls by hand. Can you imagine? Harris is a legend, though. The guy once pulled a whole family out of a second-story window by himself. But yeah, if I don't look sharp in the uniform, I just feel like I can't command that kind of respect, you know? It just throws my whole day off.
When you think about why you're so careful with food and weight, is it mostly about being thin, or is it more about staying healthy and performing well at your job?

I mean, it's definitely not about being healthy. Honestly, I'm pretty sure I'm probably less healthy now with how little I eat. It's mostly about just... being thin. Looking a certain way. I just want to be thin, you know? It's like I have this image in my head of what I'm supposed to look like, and if I don't match it, I just feel wrong. 

Which is kind of like what happened with the new engine we just got at the station. They told us we were getting this state-of-the-art pumper, right? Supposed to have this incredible turning radius and a customized cab layout. But when it actually showed up, the manufacturer had completely messed up the specs for the hose bed. It's way too high, so now the shorter guys on the crew—like Jenkins, he's barely five-foot-seven—have to practically climb the side of the truck just to rack the crosslays. Jenkins was so mad the first day we ran drills with it. He threw his helmet across the bay and it actually chipped the paint on the captain's personal truck. The captain was furious, obviously. He drives this pristine F-250, washes it every single shift. But yeah, it's really just about being thin, not about health or the job.
